title: The Engineer, the Senator and the Scientist in the 8th UAP Data Release by the U.S. Government

The 8th tranche of data on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) was released on November 20, 2026 here by the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) of the U.S. Government. It includes 40 PDF files and 3 video files and does not contain any measurement of a technology that requires a non-human origin. The three highlights of this release are Kelly Johnson’s 1953 sighting report and 1949 memo, a Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) rejection of Senator Reid’s request for a special access program (SAP), and a 1952 Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) diary entry on scientists’ papers about silent propulsion. Below are the summaries of all three items:

1. Kelly Johnson: the 1953 sighting (D206) and the 1949 memo (D213)

Clarence “Kelly” Johnson was Lockheed’s chief engineer and later designed the U-2 and SR-71. At about 5:00 p.m. on 16 December 1953, from his ranch near Agoura, California, he saw a black object above the mountains to the west. Through 8-power binoculars he watched it hold still for about three minutes, and he described it as a wing with an aspect ratio of about seven. It then left to the west in a long, shallow climb (page numbers 1, 6, 10).

At the same moment a Navy WV-2 on a Lockheed test flight, at 16,000 to 20,000 ft off the coast, also saw the object. Test pilot Roy Wimmer called out “Look out, there’s a flying saucer” (p. 9). Co-pilot Rudy Thoren flew toward it for about five minutes without closing the distance (pp. 9, 11). Chief aerodynamicist P. A. Colman saw it hover near Point Mugu for about ten minutes before it “suddenly accelerated due west” (p. 12).

The next morning Johnson stopped Thoren from telling his account until Johnson had described his own; the time and place matched (pp. 7, 10). Johnson wrote that he was “more firmly convinced than ever that such devices exist” (p. 7). An Air Force cover letter says he was “most reluctant” to file the report (p. 2). Project Blue Book classified the case as a lenticular cloud (p. 1). The release page describes D206 as a “confirmed, complete, high-quality digitization”.

Johnson also appears in D213 in another context from 1949. On 8 July 1949, as Lockheed’s Chief Research Engineer, he wrote an internal memo about a Lockheed employee, Charles E. Whitton, a former studio animator, who reported two flying discs over the San Fernando Valley on 17 June 1949. Johnson wrote: “As you know, I have been very interested in the probability of such things existing, and my discussions with certain people in the Air Force, as well as late newspaper reports indicate there is something to flying discs.” He called Whitton “definitely not a crack-pot” and asked whether the Air Force at Wright Field wanted to interview him (p. 12). The Air Materiel Command asked the Air Force plant office at Lockheed to interview Whitton “thru Mr. Clarence L. Johnson” (p. 6). Whitton described two bright metallic oval objects, seen from his car near Grand Central Airport in Glendale at 3:30 p.m. and in sight for one and a half minutes (pp. 13 to 14). The Air Force record card concludes “Aircraft” (p. 1). In his 1953 report Johnson wrote that he had “definitely believed in the possibility that flying saucers exist” for at least five years (D206, p. 7).

2. Senator Reid’s request and DIA’s answer (D183, D185, D186)

On 24 June 2009 Senator Harry Reid wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense Lynn. He cited “several highly sensitive, unconventional aerospace-related findings” and asked for a restricted special access program with a bigoted access list “for specific portions of the AATIP” (D183, p. 1). The portions he named were the methodology used to “identify, acquire, study, and engineer” the technologies, the allocation of personnel, and application and engineering (D183, pp. 1 to 2).

In November 2009 the DIA Director replied that DIA “cannot find adequate justification to establish a restricted SAP” (D185, p. 1). All program documents delivered in the first year were unclassified, and DIA was “unaware of any report containing information sufficiently sensitive” to need that protection (D185, p. 2). A later DIA memo records that Lynn and the DIA Director met Reid in November 2009 and “determined the reports were of limited value to DIA” (D186, p. 2). The files contain no approval of the program.

3. The 1952 CIA documents (D029, D027)

A CIA official diary entry of 28 October 1952 records that new information on flying saucers had been obtained, “particularly reports of sightings on the ground by relatively reliable observers”, and that “Several scientists have recently delivered papers indicating a possible means of propulsion which would not involve noise and flare” (D029). A briefing for the Air Force and the Research and Development Board was approved. The entry does not name the scientists or the papers, and the briefing is not in the release.

A CIA Office of Scientific Intelligence briefing of 14 August 1952 counts about 1,500 official reports since 1947, 250 in July 1952 alone, with 20% unexplained. It lists reported speeds up to 18,000 mph and says there is “no shred of evidence” for the interplanetary theory (D027).

4. The 1968 scientist quoted in the BAASS report (D172, p. 196)

The report quotes an “atmospheric scientist and PhD physicist”, name redacted, who said “in 1968 at his CASI lecture” that 30 to 40% of about 12,000 Blue Book cases were unexplained, “mostly military cases and many involving radar”. From 1966 on he argued with an Air Force consultant that the true number of unknowns was “about an order of magnitude” higher than the Air Force reported. The file does not print his name. Based on the public record, we assess with medium-to-high confidence that he is James E. McDonald of the University of Arizona, who spoke to the Canadian Aeronautics and Space Institute on 12 March 1968.

Other items mentioned in the release include a report (D172) with 538-pages from July 2009 by the contractor for DIA’s AAWSAP program, describing a database of 237,331 records, 26 commissioned technical papers, and a write-up of the 2004 Nimitz case (“at least 600 knots”, p. 91). It documents research into “poltergeist phenomena, discarnate voices, unusual creatures” at a Utah ranch (p. 164) and lists a goal to “Launch search to obtain EBE [extraterrestrial biology entity] tissue samples” (p. 496). It does not report any laboratory result.

In addition, a 2023 radar slide (D165) relates to a civil air-surveillance radar in the western United States, which logged eight returns over 84 seconds at an estimated 55,000 to 70,000 ft. If they are one object, it covered 38.5 miles at a minimum mean speed of 1,650 mph, about Mach 2.5. The slide states that the 12-second sweep interval “is not sufficient to independently establish” that the returns are one object. The date, radar site and raw data are withheld.

Finally, the new release also includes identifiable objects. Preliminary analysis of the 3 new video files by the UAP Science Advisory Council member, Jacob Haqq-Misra, shows one video, labeled PR168, where seven objects with periodic variation of infrared brightness as expected from birds flapping their wings (based on the algorithm discussed here) and another video, PR169, with one such bird. PR166 might also be a bird, but it is too faint and grainy to resolve in any convincing way.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Avi Loeb is chair of the UAP Science Advisory Council to the White House, Pentagon, FBI and intelligence agencies, director of the Galileo Project, founding director of Harvard University’s — Black Hole Initiative (2016–2021), former director of the Institute for Theory and Computation at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (2005–2026), and the former chair of the astronomy department at Harvard University (2011–2020). He is a former member of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (2018–2019) and a former chair of the Board on Physics and Astronomy of the National Academies (2018–2021). He is the bestselling author of “Extraterrestrial: The First Sign of Intelligent Life Beyond Earth” and a co-author of the textbook “Life in the Cosmos”, both published in 2021. The paperback edition of his new book, titled “Interstellar”, was published in August 2024.
